body:
The greatest common divisor (GCD) of two positive integers is the largest whole number that divides both without a remainder. The Euclidean algorithm finds it without factoring either number into primes.

The rule is short: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), where a mod b is the remainder left after dividing a by b. Replace the pair (a, b) with (b, a mod b) and repeat. When the remainder reaches zero, the last non-zero remainder is the GCD.

Worked example with 48 and 18: 48 divided by 18 leaves 12, so the pair becomes (18, 12). 18 divided by 12 leaves 6, giving (12, 6). 12 divided by 6 leaves 0, so the GCD is 6. Each step needs only one division, which suits pencil and paper.

The method is efficient. According to the cited source, the number of steps is proportional to the logarithm of the numbers, a result known as Lamé's theorem, so large inputs still need relatively few steps and no list of prime factors.

An extended version of the algorithm also calculates Bézout coefficients. The source describes these as essential for modular multiplicative inverses in RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC).

Limitation: this entry summarizes one cited source plus a hand-worked example. It does not prove Lamé's theorem or describe a complete cryptographic implementation.

summary: Find the greatest common divisor of two positive integers by repeatedly replacing the pair (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until the remainder is zero.
title: Find a shared divisor without factoring
